title: Enhancing the power of a quantum heat engine via control of the system--reservoir coupling
authors: Sabrina Burgardt, Julian Feß, Silvia Hiebel, Eric Lutz, Artur Widera
abstract: The non-equilibrium properties of open quantum systems are determined by the microscopic laws governing energy exchange with their environment. In particular, an enhancement of the performance of quantum heat engines has been predicted by speeding up the dynamics through control of the system--bath interaction. However, direct microscopic control of heat transfer between the machine and the reservoir has remained elusive so far. Here, we experimentally demonstrate such control in a quantum Otto engine realized with ultracold Cs-133 atoms coupled to an atomic reservoir of ultracold Rb-87 atoms. Heat exchange between the two is mediated by inelastic s-wave collisions whose energy-dependent scattering cross sections lead to an asymmetric equilibration dynamics in the isochoric heating and cooling strokes. By tuning the kinetic temperature of the atomic reservoir, we modify the associated microscopic scattering rates, and thereby the heat transfer law, giving control over the time allocation within the engine cycle through control over the microscopic, multi-exponential relaxation dynamics. This enables power output optimization at fixed efficiency. Our results establish microscopic control of system-reservoir interactions as a tool for manipulating heat flow at the nanoscale and engineering the finite-time performance of quantum thermal machines.
summary: The research experimentally demonstrates that the performance of a quantum heat engine can be optimized by controlling the system-reservoir coupling. Using ultracold atoms, the authors show that tuning the reservoir's kinetic temperature modifies the microscopic scattering rates governing heat transfer during the cycle's isochoric strokes. This provides a powerful tool for engineering finite-time energy conversion processes at the nanoscale.
main_problem: The goal is to enhance the power output of a quantum heat engine operating at finite time by microscopically controlling the energy exchange between the working system and its environment (reservoir).
main_result: The authors experimentally demonstrated that tuning the kinetic temperature of the reservoir allows for microscopic control over the heat transfer law, enabling optimization of the engine's power output while maintaining a fixed efficiency.
method: The study uses an experimental platform involving ultracold atoms to realize and measure the performance of a quantum Otto cycle, analyzing how collision-mediated energy exchange dictates the time evolution during isochoric strokes.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum Otto engine using $^{133}	ext{Cs}$ atoms as the working medium coupled to an $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atomic reservoir. Heat transfer occurs via inelastic $s$-wave collisions, which are modeled by rate matrices governing population dynamics during heating and cooling strokes.
key_observables: Power output ($P$), efficiency ($\eta$), cycle duration ($	au_{cyc}$), and the heat absorbed/released ($Q$).
important_parameters: Kinetic temperature of the reservoir ($T_{	ext{Rb}}$), magnetic field difference ($\Delta B$), and the durations of the isochoric strokes ($	au_h, 	au_c$).
main_assumptions: Adiabatic work strokes are assumed short enough that no spin-exchange collisions occur; the control mechanism relies on the asymmetric energy scaling of scattering cross-sections for different collision types.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the four-stroke cycle (isochoric heating/cooling, adiabatic expansion/compression) and show how cycle times ($	au_{cyc}$) depend strongly on $T_{	ext{Rb}}$ but weakly on $\Delta B$, while efficiency shows a monotonic dependence on $\Delta B$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework for heat exchange via collision rates, details the four-stroke cycle dynamics using master equations, and then experimentally demonstrates that tuning $T_{	ext{Rb}}$ provides the primary handle to optimize power output by controlling the relative time allocation between heating and cooling strokes.
why_interesting: This work bridges fundamental non-equilibrium thermodynamics with cutting-edge AMO physics. It shows how engineering the microscopic coupling (the reservoir interaction) can be a direct tool for optimizing macroscopic performance metrics like power in quantum engines, which is highly relevant to quantum energy technologies.
